lesson: Gate commits behind one script that exits non-zero, with set -e. A heredoc's failing exit status does not chain into the next line; two pushes went out on failed tests before this was fixed.
Never put backticks in a git -m string — bash command-substitutes them and the word vanishes from the message.
Verify a data migration on a SEEDED database with bound parameters. A ':100' inside a JSON literal in sa.text() is a bind parameter; the insert failed and the migration 'passed' on an empty table.

A balance-sheet tie-out inside one self-consistent model ties straight through a sign error. Catch sign errors with direction tests (a -95k draw must reduce cash by 95k) and the reference workbook — not with another identity.
Grading actual/target by ratio is wrong whenever the target is negative (two negatives compare magnitudes). Grade the difference in the favourable direction over |target|, in integer arithmetic.

A number is input or derived in ONE place and carried everywhere. Two copies of a formula (JS for display, stored copy for grading) guarantee drift; prove a port key-for-key before deleting the original.
create_all before Alembic creates tables the ledger doesn't know about and never alters existing ones. Migrate first on every launch; make migrations idempotent.
Don't cherry-pick files across diverged branches — it silently drops the other side's work on shared files. Merge first, then build.
When one upload shape is wrong (two Balance Sheets, no P&L) the screen looks plausible. Say it — a warning beats a screen the user has to notice is sparse.

Migration tests on SQLite do not prove Postgres. SQLite accepted a doubly-quoted JSON default that Postgres rejected, and auto-migrate then blocked the backend from starting. Compile new migrations against the Postgres dialect (a one-line check) and use sa.text() for literal server defaults.
Auto-migrate on launch turns a bad migration into 'the app will not start'. The launcher's failure message must point at the backend log, and the log must be the first thing asked for.

A $ view on a driver grid doubles as a foot-check. The moment the advisor could read the cash-flow column as dollars, three rows entered 'cash out positive' and two signed became obvious. Show the cash view early.

Pick ONE sign convention and make every line obey it. Signed cash — negative uses cash, positive adds it — lets a section sum straight down, so the reader can foot it by eye. Mixed 'natural' conventions per row hide arithmetic errors behind a correct total.

A plug is a promise you cannot audit. Overhead as 'total expenses less the named buckets' made net profit tie to QuickBooks by definition, and paid for it by double-counting any cross-section mapping and making 'Excluded' a lie. Once nothing can be unmapped, a direct sum ties by construction AND opens line by line.

A tie computed the same way is not a check — it cannot fail. Check a derived P&L against the OTHER statement: QuickBooks' cumulative net income on the balance sheet equity line. Different source, so agreement means something.

An account name is not a key. The same name legitimately owns a row on each statement (a vehicle is a fixed asset AND an expense account). Keying by name collapsed the two and the losing row's dollars silently left their category. Pair rows to results positionally, and raise if the one-per-row invariant breaks.
Test data with distinct names hid a name-collision bug that real data exposed in minutes. Ask what the fixtures quietly assume that the client's chart of accounts does not.

'Presence, not truthiness' is the house pattern for derived-unless-overridden: a key present in the override dict wins, absence lets the derivation flow. A typed zero is then a real answer and clearing a cell is how control is handed back. Used by COS pinning (025) and overhead (031).

Never pull into a running --reload dev server: it restarts mid-pull on a half-updated tree and re-runs migrations from whichever files have landed. Three launches broke this way. Make the safe order the only order — one script that stops, pulls, then launches.

A migration that alters a table waits on any session holding a lock on it, and because migrations run at app import the backend simply never answers health. Set a lock_timeout so it fails loudly, and print a progress line per startup stage.

Never connection.execute() anything in alembic/env.py before begin_transaction(). SQLAlchemy 2 auto-begins a transaction Alembic then reuses without owning, and the whole migration rolls back silently at close — with 'Running upgrade' still in the log. Session settings belong in connect_args.

A timeout is not a failure. The launcher gave up on the backend after a flat 20s while a migration over a full dataset was still running, and reported a broken app that was fine. Wait on the process being alive, not on a clock.

A liveness check must test the thing the user sees, not a proxy for it. The launcher decided an app window was open from `pgrep --user-data-dir=...`, but macOS keeps Chrome running with no windows and helper processes carry the same flag — so it reported 'brought it forward' and showed nothing while both servers sat healthy. Fourth launcher break, and the first three also came from inferring state instead of asserting it.

A build that compiles is not a build that works. A route rewrite replaced a block of App.jsx and took ten routes with it — month-header drill-downs, Import, Profile, Scenarios — and `vite build` passed clean, because an unused import is not an error. Nothing but a human clicking a month header would have found it. Assert reachability, not compilation: every imported page must appear in a Route.
